title: Vector Norm
body:
A **norm** assigns a length to a vector. Any $\|\cdot\|$ obeying three rules counts:

$$
\|\mathbf{v}\| \geq 0 \text{ with equality only at } \mathbf{0}, \qquad
\|c\mathbf{v}\| = |c|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|, \qquad
\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\| \leq \|\mathbf{u}\| + \|\mathbf{v}\|
$$

The third is the triangle inequality: no shortcut through a detour. Every norm induces a
**metric**, $d(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) = \|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\|$, so choosing a norm is
choosing what "close" means, and in this course that means **choosing a loss function**.

## The family

For $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n$:

| Norm | Formula | Unit ball | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| $L_1$ | $\sum_i \lvert v_i\rvert$ | diamond | total absolute deviation, taxicab distance |
| $L_2$ | $\sqrt{\sum_i v_i^2}$ | circle | ordinary Euclidean length |
| $L_p$ | $\left(\sum_i \lvert v_i\rvert^p\right)^{1/p}$ | interpolates | the general case |
| $L_\infty$ | $\max_i \lvert v_i\rvert$ | square | worst single component |

$L_2$ is the only one of them that comes from an [[Inner Product]] ($\|\mathbf{v}\|^2 =
\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}$). That is not a detail: it is why $L_2$ has a [[Projection]] formula,
a closed-form [[Least Squares]] solution, and a derivative everywhere, and why $L_1$ has none of
the three.

**Matrix norms** measure a matrix as an object rather than a map. The **Frobenius norm** is the
$L_2$ norm of the flattened matrix:

$$
\|A\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j} a_{ij}^2} = \sqrt{\text{tr}(A^TA)} = \sqrt{\sum_k \sigma_k^2}
$$

That last equality, Frobenius norm as the root sum of squared
[[Singular Value Decomposition|singular values]], is what makes the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem
in [[Low-Rank Approximation]] say something concrete: the error of a truncated factorisation is
the tail of the singular values you threw away. The **spectral norm** $\|A\|_2 = \sigma_1$
measures the same matrix by the worst stretch it applies to any vector instead.

## Norms as loss functions

**This is what the course is actually for.** A model produces predictions $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, the
data says $\mathbf{y}$, and the residual $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is a vector.
Training is minimising $\|\mathbf{r}\|$, and which norm you pick decides the model you get:

| Norm of the residual | Loss | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| $\|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2/n$ | **mean squared error** | differentiable, closed form, **squares outliers so they dominate** |
| $\|\mathbf{r}\|_1/n$ | **mean absolute error** | robust to outliers, no closed form, fits the median rather than the mean |
| $\|\mathbf{r}\|_\infty$ | minimax | fits the single worst case, used for guarantees rather than averages |

MSE is the default not because squaring errors is obviously right but because it is the one with
an [[Inner Product]] behind it: squaring makes the loss a smooth quadratic, its gradient is
linear, and [[Least Squares]] drops out in closed form. The cost of that convenience is the
outlier sensitivity in the middle column, and $L_1$ regression is what you switch to when the
data is dirty.

The same choice appears again in **regularisation**, penalising $\|\mathbf{w}\|$ of the weights
themselves rather than of the residual: $L_2$ (ridge) shrinks weights smoothly, $L_1$ (lasso)
drives them to exactly zero and so selects features. The corner of the $L_1$ diamond is the
geometric reason, and the smooth circle of $L_2$ is why it has no corners to land on.

Not every loss is a norm. [[Cross-Entropy Loss]] and [[Log Loss]] measure disagreement between
probability distributions, not distance between vectors, which is why classification uses them
and regression uses these. See [[Loss Function]] and [[Gradient Descent]], which minimises
whichever one you chose.
